passage: Ivan had been in Porto for six weeks when the electricity bill arrived in the shared flat, much higher than he'd guessed. He and Diego sat at the kitchen table with the letter between them. "I thought it was included in rent," Ivan said, his ears going red. It wasn't. He opened his banking app and scrolled: late-night takeaways, a jacket, three concert tickets. No wonder his account looked thin. For the first time there was no parent to call and quietly top it up. That night he made a simple spreadsheet: rent, bills, groceries, travel, fun. He set aside his half of the bill first, then cut the takeaways to one a week. Diego laughed. "You're scarier than my mum." Ivan grinned, a little tired. "I have to be my own mum now."

qa.q: In which city was Ivan living with Diego?
qa.a: In Porto.

qa.q: Why did Ivan's ears go red at the kitchen table?
qa.a: He was embarrassed to realise he had misunderstood the rent and had been spending without tracking, with no parent to fix it.

qa.q: Which change in Ivan's plan is most useful, and why?
qa.a: Setting aside the bill money before anything else, because it makes sure fixed costs are covered before spending on extras.

qa.q: How might Diego feel about Ivan's new spreadsheet?
qa.a: He teases him but is probably relieved, since a flatmate who pays his share on time makes sharing a home much easier. 😅

grounding: Shows a young adult abroad learning to budget and manage bills without parental support.

passage: The college hostel office pinned the mess-fee list on the notice board, and Arohi's name was on it in red: unpaid. Her face went hot. Her scholarship money had arrived in the first week and somehow vanished into printouts, canteen coffees and an online sale. She hadn't told her parents; they had already stretched to pay her admission. In the reading room, Vaibhav, a final-year student who helped juniors with forms, noticed her staring at nothing. "Mess fee?" he asked. She nodded. He pulled out a small notebook of his own, every rupee written down. "First week, fixed things. Then everything else," he said. That evening Arohi paid the fee from what was left, wrote a list of fixed costs, and set a weekly limit for the canteen.

qa.q: Where did Arohi see her name marked as unpaid?
qa.a: On the notice board, where the hostel office pinned the mess-fee list.

qa.q: Why hadn't Arohi told her parents about the money trouble?
qa.a: She felt guilty because they had already stretched to pay her admission, and she did not want to burden or disappoint them.

qa.q: What small step from Vaibhav helped Arohi most?
qa.a: His rule of paying fixed costs first gave her a simple order to follow, turning her panic into a plan.

qa.q: What is it like for Vaibhav when he sees juniors like Arohi struggling?
qa.a: He seems to remember his own learning, which is why he shares his notebook calmly and without judgment.

grounding: Shows a college student learning to manage her own expenses after overspending, with a senior's practical tip.

passage:
Subject: adulting update (send help)

Hi Lavanya,

First stipend from the internship came in on Monday! I felt rich for exactly two days.

Then reality: rent to the landlady, the electricity bill I forgot (with a late fee, ugh 😩), metro card top-up, and my share of the gas cylinder. When I added it all up, most of the stipend was already gone.

So I've started a tiny system. On the day money comes, I pay rent and bills first, put a little aside in a separate account, and then split what's left into weekly envelopes. Food, travel, and a "fun" envelope that I'm allowed to spend guilt-free.

Papa offered to send money. I said no. I want to see if I can manage on my own.

How are you doing with yours?

Aadhya

passage: 'Binita, okay, confession. First month in Bengaluru, I ran out of money on the nineteenth. No idea where it went. So I sat with my bank messages and a notebook for a whole Sunday. Rent, electricity, mess fee, fine. Then thirty-one food deliveries. Thirty-one! And three subscriptions I forgot I'd started. I felt sick, honestly. I didn't want to call home for money; Appa's already stretched. So now, the day my stipend comes, rent and bills go out first. What's left I keep in envelopes, actual cash, one for each week. When a week's envelope is empty, I cook rice and eggs. It's boring. But last month I had eleven hundred left over, and I didn't have to ask anyone.'

passage: I'm Vandana. I share a flat in Pune with Shreya, and I've watched her change since June. At first, bills just piled up on the fridge. The electricity got cut once, for a whole evening, because a payment slipped. She didn't cry, but she went very quiet and sat on the floor with a calculator. Now there's a whiteboard by the door with every due date and a tick beside each. She splits the internet bill with me on the first, exact to the rupee, and shows me the receipt. Last week her parents offered to send extra, and I heard her say, 'No, Mummy, I've got it this month.' I don't know if she was sure. She checked the whiteboard twice after the call.

qa.q: Where is the whiteboard?
qa.a: By the door.

qa.q: What might Shreya checking the whiteboard twice after the call suggest?
qa.a: It may suggest she felt unsure and a little anxious about managing, even though she wanted to handle it herself.

qa.q: What could help Shreya if a month gets tight?
qa.a: She could keep tracking dues and, if money runs short, talk honestly with her parents rather than letting bills slip.

qa.q: How does Vandana benefit from Shreya's new system?
qa.a: Bills are split on time and shown clearly, so there is less stress and no more surprise power cuts.

passage: First month in Bengaluru: Vikas, nineteen, had his first stipend and no parents watching. By the twentieth, he was eating instant noodles and borrowing from his flatmate Devika. Third month: he paid the electricity bill the day it arrived, split the Wi-Fi fairly with Devika, and cooked rice and dal three nights a week. passage: Sunaina had been in her Bengaluru PG for one month when she opened her notebook and added up the numbers. Rent, the metro card, the phone bill, groceries. Then the food delivery column: far bigger than she'd guessed. She stared at it, stomach tight. Her stipend came on the first; it was the twenty-fourth. Her colleague Harish, who shared the same metro route, noticed her quiet at lunch. "Month-end blues?" She laughed awkwardly and told him. He didn't lecture. "I made a list my first year of what I actually need versus what's just tired-night ordering. Helped me see it." That evening, Sunaina cooked poha in the PG kitchen, wrote "cook three nights a week" in her notebook, and set a reminder for rent.

"Mridul, the electricity bill came. It's huge."
"How huge, Sarita?"
"Double last month."

"And your heater for bathing! We both used it."
"Okay, okay. Let's not fight. How do we split it?"
"Half-half like always?"
"But you were away for ten days."
Sarita paused. "Fair. So I pay less?"
"Maybe we make a sheet. Rent half, internet half, electricity by days here."
"And the gas cylinder?"
"Same sheet. And we both put reminders for due dates, so no late fee like in June."
Sarita grinned. "Look at us. Adults."
"Barely," Mridul said, opening a new spreadsheet.

passage:
Hostel mentor's note, first-year students, October
Sharmila came to see me after her phone was cut off for an unpaid bill. It was her first time handling money without her parents; they send an amount at the start of each month.
She showed me her spending. Most of it went in the first ten days on food delivery and a trip with friends. She was embarrassed and near tears. "At home I never even saw the bills."
Her roommate Bidisha, who works part-time, showed her how she writes every expense in a notebook each night.
I did not tell Sharmila what to spend. I suggested she list her fixed bills first and talk to the college's student finance advisor, who runs free sessions.
She booked one for Monday.

qa.q: When did most of Sharmila's money go?
qa.a: In the first ten days, on food delivery and a trip with friends.

qa.q: How did Sharmila feel when she showed her spending?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and close to tears.

qa.q: What made the mentor's advice helpful?
qa.a: The mentor pointed Sharmila to list fixed bills and see the student finance advisor, instead of setting a money rule personally.

qa.q: How might Bidisha feel sharing her notebook method?
qa.a: Bidisha may feel glad and a little proud to help, having learned to manage money through her part-time job.

grounding: A mentor's note on a young adult learning to manage bills and spending on her own.

passage:
29 Aug
Rent day again. First year in my own room, and I still sweat on rent day.
I've started doing what Minakshi from my office showed me: on salary day I pay rent, electricity and the phone first, before I even think about eating out. Then whatever's left is what's left.
This month the electricity bill came double because of the heat. I felt the panic rise, the old urge to call home. I didn't. I cooked more at home, skipped the weekend movie, and made it.
I felt oddly proud washing my own dal pot tonight.
I still don't understand how insurance works. Minakshi said to ask the bank's help desk, not a random video. Next Saturday.
Nilesh

qa.a: Rent, electricity and the phone.

qa.a: Nilesh felt panic rise and the urge to call home, then later felt proud of managing.

qa.a: Asking the bank's help desk about insurance, because it is a qualified source rather than a random video.

passage: Anirban's first month as a junior clerk at the block office in Bolpur ended with ₹340 left and three days to go. He sat on the thin mattress in his rented room and opened the notebook he'd started. Rent, paid. Electricity, paid on time at the post office. Mess food, fine. But the column marked "snacks and tea" was longer than he'd expected: small cups, every hour, with anyone who asked. His landlady's daughter Ganga, who kept her mother's shop accounts, looked over his shoulder when she brought the water bill. "The tea's eating you alive," she laughed. That night he drew a line: a flask from his room each morning. Next month, he wrote, the notebook decides, not the tea stall.

qa.a: He had ₹340 left with three days to go.

qa.q: How did Anirban feel looking at the "snacks and tea" column?

qa.q: What choice did Anirban make, and who else could help him plan?
